[0] To understand wave propagation, we need to follow individual particles of the medium.
We begin with a transverse wave traveling along an elastic cord.
[1] Every short segment of the cord has both mass and elasticity.
When the cord bends, elastic forces act across its cross sections.
    break: {"before":"To understand wave propagation, we need to follow individual particles of the medium.\nWe begin with a transverse wave traveling along an elastic cord.","after":"Every short segment of the cord has both mass and elasticity.\nWhen the cord bends, elastic forces act across its cross sections."}
[2] The net restoring force tends to pull each segment toward equilibrium.
Inertia carries a moving segment past its equilibrium position.
    break: {"before":"Every short segment of the cord has both mass and elasticity.\nWhen the cord bends, elastic forces act across its cross sections.","after":"The net restoring force tends to pull each segment toward equilibrium.\nInertia carries a moving segment past its equilibrium position."}
[3] Beyond equilibrium, the restoring force slows its outward motion.
At maximum displacement it stops briefly, then starts back.
    break: {"before":"The net restoring force tends to pull each segment toward equilibrium.\nInertia carries a moving segment past its equilibrium position.","after":"Beyond equilibrium, the restoring force slows its outward motion.\nAt maximum displacement it stops briefly, then starts back."}
[4] Figure 69 models the cord with a chain of identical metal balls.
The balls hang from strings and are joined by springs.
The springs have much less mass than the balls.
    break: {"before":"Beyond equilibrium, the restoring force slows its outward motion.\nAt maximum displacement it stops briefly, then starts back.","after":"Figure 69 models the cord with a chain of identical metal balls.\nThe balls hang from strings and are joined by springs.\nThe springs have much less mass than the balls."}
[5] Most of the model's mass is concentrated in the balls.
The light springs provide elastic coupling.
This captures the basic wave mechanism, not every detail of a real cord.
    break: {"before":"Figure 69 models the cord with a chain of identical metal balls.\nThe balls hang from strings and are joined by springs.\nThe springs have much less mass than the balls.","after":"Most of the model's mass is concentrated in the balls.\nThe light springs provide elastic coupling.\nThis captures the basic wave mechanism, not every detail of a real cord."}
[6] Move the leftmost ball sideways in the horizontal plane.
Here, sideways means perpendicular to the chain.
The connecting spring deforms and pulls the second ball sideways.
    break: {"before":"Most of the model's mass is concentrated in the balls.\nThe light springs provide elastic coupling.\nThis captures the basic wave mechanism, not every detail of a real cord.","after":"Move the leftmost ball sideways in the horizontal plane.\nHere, sideways means perpendicular to the chain.\nThe connecting spring deforms and pulls the second ball sideways."}
[7] That ball has inertia, so its response takes time.
Its motion follows the first ball's motion with a delay.
    break: {"before":"Move the leftmost ball sideways in the horizontal plane.\nHere, sideways means perpendicular to the chain.\nThe connecting spring deforms and pulls the second ball sideways.","after":"That ball has inertia, so its response takes time.\nIts motion follows the first ball's motion with a delay."}
[8] This is an ideal small-amplitude model, before appreciable loss or reflection.
    break: {"before":"That ball has inertia, so its response takes time.\nIts motion follows the first ball's motion with a delay.","after":"This is an ideal small-amplitude model, before appreciable loss or reflection."}
[9] Drive the first ball periodically with period $T$, by hand or a mechanism.
The second ball is forced to oscillate, with a phase delay.
    break: {"before":"This is an ideal small-amplitude model, before appreciable loss or reflection.","after":"Drive the first ball periodically with period $T$, by hand or a mechanism.\nThe second ball is forced to oscillate, with a phase delay."}
[10] Through the next spring, the third ball responds with a further delay.
The disturbance continues from ball to ball along the chain.
    break: {"before":"Drive the first ball periodically with period $T$, by hand or a mechanism.\nThe second ball is forced to oscillate, with a phase delay.","after":"Through the next spring, the third ball responds with a further delay.\nThe disturbance continues from ball to ball along the chain."}
[11] After the initial transient, the driven balls share the driving frequency.
Before reflected waves return, this is an outgoing transverse wave.
    break: {"before":"Through the next spring, the third ball responds with a further delay.\nThe disturbance continues from ball to ball along the chain.","after":"After the initial transient, the driven balls share the driving frequency.\nBefore reflected waves return, this is an outgoing transverse wave."}
[12] Figure 70 has six overhead views of the ball positions, labeled a, b, c, d, e, and f.
The views are a quarter-cycle apart, and each arrow is a ball's velocity vector.
    break: {"before":"After the initial transient, the driven balls share the driving frequency.\nBefore reflected waves return, this is an outgoing transverse wave.","after":"Figure 70 has six overhead views of the ball positions, labeled a, b, c, d, e, and f.\nThe views are a quarter-cycle apart, and each arrow is a ball's velocity vector."}
[13] Figure 71a uses heavy balls connected by light springs.
The suspension lets each ball oscillate only along the chain.
Drive the first ball with period $T$ along that same direction.
    break: {"before":"Figure 70 has six overhead views of the ball positions, labeled a, b, c, d, e, and f.\nThe views are a quarter-cycle apart, and each arrow is a ball's velocity vector.","after":"Figure 71a uses heavy balls connected by light springs.\nThe suspension lets each ball oscillate only along the chain.\nDrive the first ball with period $T$ along that same direction."}
[14] A longitudinal wave then travels along the chain.
Close and wide gaps between balls form compressions and rarefactions.
Figure 71b shows the pattern as each ball oscillates locally.
